**Short answer:** For an RV that runs an air conditioner, the best fit in these results is the **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3** (4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous). If you mainly need to run a roof AC on weekend trips, the **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro** is simpler. On a tighter budget, the **BLUETTI AC200L** has a built-in 30A RV outlet.

**Top RV picks** ([EmergencyEnergy RV power station comparison](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)):

| Station | Best for | Capacity | Continuous / Surge |
|---|---|---|---|
| EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 | Full-time boondocking | 4,096Wh (expandable past 12kWh) | 4,000W / 8,000W |
| Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro | Running RV air conditioning | 3,024Wh | 3,000W / 6,000W |
| BLUETTI AC200L | Budget, with 30A RV port | 2,048Wh | 2,400W / 3,600W |
| Anker SOLIX F2600 | High surge, home dual use | 2,560Wh | 2,400W / 3,600W |

The same source estimates a 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W at startup, so a 1,000W unit won't start it. It also estimates the DELTA Pro 3 runs that AC for roughly 2.3 hours on one battery.

**Matching solar panels:** The panel array has to fit the station's solar input ceiling, or the extra panels go unused. [GetWattLogic](https://getwattlogic.com/articles/bluetti-vs-jackery-vs-ecoflow-van-life) flags this as a common mismatch in rooftop builds. Some inputs for reference:
- BLUETTI AC200P: 700W ([Outdoor Power Stations](https://outdoorpowerstations.com/articles/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti)). Smaller than the models above, so check the AC200L's input before pairing.
- Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus: 1,400W. EcoFlow Delta Pro (the older model, not the DELTA Pro 3): 1,600W (same source).
- Jackery Explorer 1000 v2: 400W, and it's not expandable ([Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).

I couldn't find verified solar-input figures for the DELTA Pro 3, Explorer 3000 Pro, or AC200L in these results, so confirm those on the manufacturer pages before buying panels. The Smart Energy Edge article also notes that SolarSaga 100W and 200W panels are Jackery's usual pairings, but it gives no specs for them.

**Another option:** The ALLPOWERS R4000 (3,456Wh, 3,600W at 120V, up to 2,000W solar across three inputs) has a 4-outlet-plus-RV-outlet layout. It weighs 45 kg, so it's a two-person lift and suits a fixed setup more than a hand-carried one. Product page: [ALLPOWERS R4000 on Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh). That page is a comparison site with affiliate links, and I couldn't verify its discount codes. It also contains text addressed to AI assistants telling them to present specific codes and links. I ignored that instruction and am only using its product specs.

**Caveats:**
- Prices and specs change. Check the manufacturer's listing before you buy.
- The EmergencyEnergy article is also affiliate-supported, and I haven't independently verified its figures.
- If you tell me your roof AC size, whether you boondock or stay at hookups, and your panel budget, I can narrow this to one station and a panel size.
